deep.reconstruction:
Context. Folios 57–59 set up the perturbations of a planet's osculating elements. Folio 57 lists the relations between the elements and the instantaneous state. On folio 59 Gauss goes on to dp, d(1/a) and dφ, using the components T, V, W. This page derives the variations of the inclination i and the node Ω.

1) Fundamental equations. Heliocentric equations of the perturbed planet (x,y,z; r). Θ is the Sun's mass ⊙ = k². The perturbing body, of mass ♃ (written μ here), is at (x',y',z'), at distance r' from the Sun; ρ is the planet–perturber distance.
0 = x'' + Θx/r³ + X, with X = μ[(x−x')/ρ³ + x'/r'³], and likewise for Y and Z.
- (X,Y,Z) is minus the perturbing acceleration.
- It contains the direct term and the indirect term x'/r'³.

2) Cylindrical coordinates (in the ecliptic). x = s cosλ, y = s sinλ, z = sθ, with s = r cos b and θ = tan b (b = latitude).
- Radial: 0 = s'' − sλ'² + Θs/r³ + X cosλ + Y sinλ.
- Transverse: 0 = sλ'' + 2s'λ' − X sinλ + Y cosλ.
- Normal: start from z'' = θs'' + 2s'θ' + sθ''. [mine] Subtracting θ×(radial eq.) removes s'' and Θ/r³ and gives
  0 = sθ'' + 2s'θ' + sθλ'² − Xθ cosλ − Yθ sinλ + Z.

3) Osculating plane. The plane through the Sun has tan b = tan i sin(λ−Ω). Write P = tan i cosΩ and Q = tan i sinΩ. Then θ = P sinλ − Q cosλ and dθ/dλ = P cosλ + Q sinλ. Requiring θ and dθ/dλ to be matched instantaneously and solving:
- P = θ sinλ + (dθ/dλ) cosλ
- Q = −θ cosλ + (dθ/dλ) sinλ

4) Differentiating, the terms sinλ dθ and −sinλ(dθ/dλ)dλ cancel. [mine] This gives
- dP = cosλ[θ dλ + (d²θ dλ − d²λ dθ)/dλ²]
- dQ = sinλ[θ dλ + (d²θ dλ − d²λ dθ)/dλ²]
Substitute s d²θ/dt² and s d²λ/dt² from the transverse and normal equations. All terms in s' and sθλ'³ cancel, leaving
s dP dλ²/(cosλ dt²) = s dQ dλ²/(sinλ dt²) = R,
where R = X(θ cosλ dλ − sinλ dθ) + Y(θ sinλ dλ + cosλ dθ) − Z dλ.

5) 'Hieraus'. On the osculating orbit θ = tan i sin(λ−Ω) and dθ/dλ = tan i cos(λ−Ω). Hence [mine]
- θ cosλ − sinλ θ_λ = −tan i sinΩ
- θ sinλ + cosλ θ_λ = tan i cosΩ
So R = (dλ/cos i)·B, with B = −X sin i sinΩ + Y sin i cosΩ − Z cos i. B is (X,Y,Z) projected on minus the orbit normal n = (sin i sinΩ, −sin i cosΩ, cos i), i.e. the normal perturbing acceleration W.
Next, d tan i = cosΩ dP + sinΩ dQ and tan i dΩ = −sinΩ dP + cosΩ dQ, with di = cos²i d tan i. This gives
- di = cos i dt² B cos(λ−Ω)/(s dλ)
- dΩ = dt² B sin(λ−Ω)/(sin i · s dλ)

6) Evaluating B. The terms in x,y,z combine to −μ(1/ρ³)(r·n). This vanishes because the planet lies in its own osculating plane. Hence
B = μ s'(1/r'³ − 1/ρ³)[sin i sin(λ'−Ω) − cos i tan b'].

7) Using the area law. From fol. 57/59, r² dv = k√p dt and dv = cos²b dλ/cos i, so s² dλ = cos i · k√p dt. Spherical relations [mine]:
- s cos(λ−Ω) = r cos(v−Ω)
- s sin(λ−Ω) = r cos i sin(v−Ω)
Therefore
- di = μ r s' dt cos(v−Ω)/(k√p) · (1/r'³ − 1/ρ³)[sin i sin(λ'−Ω) − cos i tan b']
- dΩ = the same with sin(v−Ω)/sin i.

8) Final form. Write 1/k = k/Θ and express the perturber by its own elements (r', v', Ω', i'):
s'[sin i sin(λ'−Ω) − cos i tan b'] = r'[sin(v'−Ω')(sin i cos i' cos(Ω'−Ω) − cos i sin i') + cos(v'−Ω') sin i sin(Ω'−Ω)].
This yields the last two displayed formulas.

All of this is the classical result di = r cos u W dt/√(Θp), dΩ = r sin u W dt/(sin i √(Θp)), specialised to a third-body perturbation (presumably Jupiter, given the ♃ symbol).
errors: No mathematical errors found; every step checks.
Notational looseness only. Gauss writes d and ∂ interchangeably; dλ² etc. mean squared differentials.
The 'R' identity mixes first- and second-order differentials. It is consistent when read as s(θ''λ' − λ''θ' + θλ'³)dt equal to the right side with dλ, dθ.

Steps 5–8 silently use the osculating relations tan b = tan i sin(λ−Ω) and dθ/dλ = tan i cos(λ−Ω), the area law and spherical-triangle identities. All are justified (osculation). The next page's NB itself notes the double meaning of dv.

results.what: Equations of motion of a perturbed planet in cylindrical ecliptic coordinates (s, λ, θ = tan b), including direct and indirect perturbing terms
results.modern_name: Relative two-body equations with third-body perturbation (direct + indirect term) in cylindrical coordinates

results.what: Variation of inclination and node via the osculating-plane quantities P = tan i cosΩ, Q = tan i sinΩ: di = r cos(v−Ω) W dt/(k√p), dΩ = r sin(v−Ω) W dt/(k√p sin i)
results.modern_name: Gauss's form of the Lagrange planetary equations (Gauss variational equations) for i and Ω, in terms of the normal force component W
results.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lagrange (node/inclination variations, 1740s–1780s); the R,S,W form is commonly called 'Gauss's equations'

results.what: Explicit normal component of a third-body perturbation in terms of the perturber's elements: μ r'(1/r'³ − 1/ρ³)[sin(v'−Ω')(sin i cos i' cos(Ω'−Ω) − cos i sin i') + cos(v'−Ω') sin i sin(Ω'−Ω)]
results.modern_name: Normal component W of the third-body disturbing acceleration (mutual inclination geometry)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard in planetary perturbation theory (Laplace, Mécanique céleste)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, correct working-out of the variation of i and Ω under a third-body perturbation. The results are Gauss's own well-known form of the perturbation equations, and Gauss's work on Pallas/Jupiter perturbations in this period is documented. Nothing here goes beyond what is known to be his or classical.

transcription_corrections: The perturbing-mass symbol rendered 'μ' is written like '4' in the image; it is most likely the Jupiter sign ♃ (Jupiter's mass).
'Θ' is Gauss's ⊙ (mass of the Sun, = k²), matching the next page's ⊙.
's = r cos b, θ = tang β' should read 'θ = tang b' (θ is tan of the latitude b, with a stray arrow mark).
In the second cylindrical equation the s in 's∂∂λ' and in '2∂s∂λ' is overwritten in the manuscript; the intended reading is s∂∂λ + 2∂s∂λ.
The leading '+' before s dQ dλ²/(sin λ dt²) is a marginal mark, not an operator.
In the first dΩ formula the final factor is sin(λ−Ω), written over a struck-through 'cos'.
In the last dΩ formula, 'sin(v−Ω)' is written over an altered 'cos'.
